RagShortTexts: Weave, surface dressing and seams affect rain shedding; wet clothes still grow heavy and cold.
Wax or oil treatments cost materials and care and do not imply universal waterproof clothing.

Variants.Content:
In rain, travelers try to cover head, shoulders, baggage and dry contents. A close weave and suitable overlap shed some water, while necks, ties and seams still leak. Wax or oily dressing costs materials and work and wears or collects dirt, requiring maintenance. Cloth and thickness vary, so a cloak’s name alone does not establish protection.

Wet clothes make cold wind harder to endure and add weight. Drying needs shelter alongside food and lodging. Fire can scorch garments or stain them with tar, while spare clothes also need protection. Wealthy travelers have replacements and servants; poor walkers balance progress, delays and lodging, valuing even one dry layer.
Outfitting retainers needs fit, wind cover and repairability rather than a waxed label. Spares, needles and shelter also cost resources.
Escorts keep spare wraps and rations dry separately. A wet cloak against food spoils both; night travel needs a drying destination.
Mending needs thread, patches and time, while wax competes with lighting and sale. Lending dry clothes leaves the lender short of a garment.
